The aspect of Dr. Rappaccini's control over his daughter has caught my attention while reading Rappaccini's Daughter. Right from Beatrice’s childhood, her father raised her in a garden full of lethal flora which consequently made her immune to the plant’s poison but made her very self lethal to any living thing. It's important to note that Beatrice never approved such a thing to happen but her father conducted these experiments because of his science.

This situation reminds me of the real life case of Chinese scientist He Jiankui, who created what became known as the CRISPR babies. In 2018, Jiankui modified the DNA of human embryos using CRISPR technology and made babies resistant to HIV infection. Two twin girls and then another baby boy were born due to this experiment. Inappropriate actions of the researcher, such as lacking ethics board approval and incomplete consent of parents, violated the law and led to illegal practice of medicine, for which he was sentenced to 3 years in jail (Marchione, 2019).

There are some obvious similarities between this story and the events related to Beatrice. In both stories, a scientist performs an experiment with a person's biological identity without obtaining permission or refusal from the person. Beatrice cannot decide whether she would become a poisonous person and CRISPR babies had no ability to refuse having their DNA changed. Second similarity is that both experiments have irreversible consequences; Beatrice remains poisonous forever, CRISPR babies inherit modified DNA throughout their lives.

During the 19th century, a man had the power to commit his wife to a mental institution without any approval from her, a hearing, or actual proof of her illness. At the same time, men were supposed to go through a jury trial before being admitted to a mental institution. Such an occurrence happened to Elizabeth Packard in 1860. Packard was committed by her husband according to Illinois law because of her disagreement with the man's religion. She was kept in a mental hospital for three years before a jury trial lasted only seven minutes and declared her sane (Illinois Courts).

Today, only people who are dangerous to themselves or others may be committed involuntarily. Besides that, they are granted a hearing and an attorney (Congressional Research Service). The biggest difference is that today everyone gets the same due process no matter their sex or marital status. However, there are several aspects which remain the same. People in a mental health crisis can still be committed against their will today, and there's still debate over how much power doctors and family members should have when a patient disagrees with their treatment.

In high school, I took AP US History, and the Civil War was taught through battles, leaders, slavery, and political aspects only. I do not remember learning much about medicine. If it came up, it was a quick mention of amputations or how many soldiers died. I never learned how the medical side actually worked. The thing that surprised me the most in Ina Dixon's article, Modern Medicine's Civil War Legacy, is the large number of soldiers who died not on the battlefield but from infections and illnesses. Dysentery, typhoid fever, and pneumonia spread widely among the army because of poor hygiene and unhealthy diet of soldiers. Moreover, bloodletting and mercury were applied as methods of treatment at the beginning of the war.

In my opinion, the most valuable legacy of the war in terms of medicine is the development of an organized healthcare system. The Army of the Potomac got an organized system of care thanks to Jonathan Letterman, who created an ambulance and evacuation process. Triage, the treatment based on the level of urgency, developed. Hospitals started working in an organized manner; there were leaders such as William Hammond and Clara Barton who established certain standards of care.

The use of anesthesia during surgery was also widely used during the Civil War period. These concepts are still used today. The system of triage is used in emergency departments, and ambulances transport the patients to hospitals. As a student studying information technology, I see the importance of the system of evacuation and its efficiency. Also, during this time period thousands of doctors and nurses gained valuable experience during the war.

While reading the story by Anton Chekhov “A Doctor’s Visit,” I could not help but compare it to the piano composition “Opening” by Philip Glass. The repeating melody creates an impression of anxiety, as though one was trying to move forward but remaining stuck in one’s own thoughts. It makes me think of Liza’s sleepless nights and the overall atmosphere of anxiety around the factory. Although there is no production due to the holiday, the constant metal strikes of the watchman interrupt the silence.

In the process of reading Eudora Welty's "A Worn Path," I found similarities between the text and Lange's photograph called "Migrant Mother." The picture represents a mother with her children around her. While gazing at something far away, she puts one hand on her face. Two children lean against her shoulders while she holds an infant. The first aspect that caught my attention was the children's dependence on her and her worried and exhausted look. In connection with the text, I thought about Phoenix Jackson taking care of her ill grandson. Even though he is her grandson and not a son, the same feeling of having to care for somebody else came to mind while analyzing these two works. Though it is hard to say what the woman is thinking from her expression, I see worry and determination in her expression, which reminds me of Phoenix.
